numeric_source_review_queue.text: \noindent Can public market data identify destabilizing algorithmic feedback, and when does feedback threaten dealer solvency? We establish two fundamental limits. First, under the declared reset price-response contract, the model identifies merged rate--weight representations, with an $\Omega(\delta^{-4})$ sample complexity lower bound for distinguishing nearby adaptation rates; the scalar Gaussian experiment yields a finite-window abstention bound near its unit-root boundary. Empirically, measured feedback is dominated by filtering choices: raw-return feedback intervals span zero, and covariance restrictions reject ($J=73.0, df=4$). Second, spectral price stability ($\rho(J)<1$) does not prevent dealer balance-sheet exhaustion under non-normal transient amplification ($r^* = B / \sup_{t \ge 0} \|C J^t\|_2$). Funded dealer simulations illustrate that capital solvency fails inside the spectrally stable regime, motivating capital-aware pre-trade gating.

numeric_source_review_queue.text: The delegation of financial execution and market making to autonomous algorithms has fundamentally transformed the microstructural physics of modern electronic exchanges. Over the past three decades, financial markets have undergone an unprecedented structural transition from human-intermediated floor trading and manual specialist posts (such as the historic open-outcry pits of Chicago and the specialist trading posts of the New York Stock Exchange) to fully automated, electronic continuous double auctions housed in co-located server racks in Secaucus, New Jersey (Equinix NY4) and Slough, United Kingdom (Equinix LD4). In contemporary equity, sovereign debt, foreign exchange, and digital asset venues, automated execution engines, statistical arbitrageurs, and high-frequency market makers (HFMs) submit and cancel the overwhelming majority of limit quotes, respond to order flow in microseconds, and continuously adapt their execution strategies to prevailing market conditions \citep{hasbrouck1991,menkveld2013,budish2015,biais2015}.
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: When trading algorithms condition their order submission and quote-placement decisions on recent transaction prices, prevailing order book imbalances, and trade innovations, the price-formation process ceases to be an open-loop mechanism driven purely by exogenous informational updates regarding fundamentals. Instead, price formation becomes an autonomous \emph{closed-loop dynamical system}: trading decisions generate endogenous price impact, and the resulting price adjustments directly feed back into the learning rules, momentum filters, risk-budgeting heuristics, and execution programs of competing market participants \citep{bouchaud2004fluctuations,cont2010stochastic,cont2014}.
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: This closed-loop structural reality was dramatically underscored by major episodic disruptions in electronic markets over the past decade and a half. While disruptions such as the May 6, 2010 Flash Crash in the E-mini S\&P 500 and the October 15, 2014 Treasury flash rally provide compelling historical motivation for analyzing how algorithmic feedback can rapidly deplete liquidity, direct empirical investigation of these episodes is constrained by the non-public nature of regulatory account registries. Modern electronic cryptocurrency order books provide an ideal, transparent empirical testing ground. Electronic cryptocurrency venues provide public trade and book data, but these records do not identify the fraction of activity generated by adaptive algorithms. The supplied samples have the clocks and coverage described below; they do not establish universal nanosecond observation or the absence of off-exchange execution. We therefore exploit high-frequency cryptocurrency order books (complemented by a benchmark sample of regulated NASDAQ Nordic equities) as an empirical testing ground for our broader theoretical framework.

numeric_source_review_queue.text: \paragraph{Pillar 1: Observable Feedback Does Not Imply Identifiable Machine Behavior.}
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: We establish what public price and order-flow data can and cannot reveal about underlying learning algorithms. Within the specified reset linear market--learning contract with known anchor and impact, modeled aggregate price-state responses identify the \emph{merged rate--weight representation}. Individual algorithmic cohorts that share common adaptation rates cannot be distinguished from public price feeds—an exact realization-theoretic equivalence class (Theorem~\ref{thm:m1_equivalence}). Furthermore, detecting heterogeneity between two cohorts whose adaptation timescales differ by a small margin $\delta$ requires an active probing budget growing at the severe sample-complexity rate of $\Omega(\delta^{-4})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:m2_sample_complexity}). In the stated scalar Gaussian price experiment, finite-window classifiers with uniform error control have a positive abstention-probability bound near its unit-root boundary (Theorem~\ref{thm:m3_minimax_abstention}). An additional economic contract gives conditions under which uncertainty about adverse-mark costs raises a robust break-even quote and reduces allocation surplus (Proposition~\ref{thm:welfare_opacity}). The cohort-equivalence result alone does not imply a positive spread premium or a market welfare loss.
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: Crucially, we show that this identification boundary extends to empirical measurement: estimated feedback parameters are fragile artifacts of microstructural observation clocks and state definitions. Using continuous high-frequency limit order books and a multi-year panel of 768 asset-days on Binance Spot (2021--2024), we show that while an exponentially smoothed price-deviation proxy exhibits modest positive autocorrelation ($\hat{Q} \approx 0.008$), this parameter measures mean-reversion toward a trailing moving-average anchor rather than fundamental mispricing. When order flow is properly aligned with past observed intervals, feedback drops to $\hat{Q} \approx 0.0019$, and when the state is defined as raw price returns, empirical feedback intervals uniformly span zero. Furthermore, dynamic minimum-distance covariance matching formally rejects the parsimonious linear model ($J = 73.0, df = 4, p < 0.001$), while Rigobon heteroskedasticity identification reveals negative contemporaneous buffering ($Q_{\text{Rig}} = -0.0191$). As a structural stress calibration, we examine the system's response to the July 8, 2022 Binance zero-fee schedule overhaul ($N=192$): eliminating taker fees sparked a $+75.01\%$ volume surge without detectable feedback persistence amplification ($\hat{\beta}_3 = -0.00186, p = 0.547$, permutation $p = 0.750$), calibrating the system's subcritical stability bounds under extreme volume expansion.

Because the closed-loop market Jacobian $J$ is generically non-normal under asymmetric price-impact and memory parameters (with $J J^\top - J^\top J \neq 0$ except on a measure-zero algebraic subvariety), stable eigenvalues can coexist with massive transient balance-sheet excursion. The exact worst-case safe shock radius for a leveraged dealer is governed by peak transient magnification:

numeric_source_review_queue.text: proving that $\frac{B}{e n \mathcal{K}(J)}$ provides a guaranteed safe lower bound, whereas $\frac{B}{\mathcal{K}(J)}$ is an upper bound that must never be mistaken for a conservative safety threshold. In complementary simulation environments ($N = 19{,}200$ paths across 48 cells), we evaluate dealer capital solvency strictly inside the spectrally stable regime ($\rho(J) \in [0.80, 0.985] < 1.0$), demonstrating that dealer solvency failure surges from $11.0\%$ to $100.0\%$ as feedback increases, driven by $(1 - S)^{-2}$ low-frequency variance inflation. This structural divergence motivates capital-aware pre-trade gating grounded in the exact safe radius $r^*_{\text{exact}} = B/M_C$.

numeric_source_review_queue.text: Beginning with the seminal contributions of \citet{kyle1985continuous} and \citet{glosten1985bid}, classical microstructure models analyze the informational content of order flow and dealer inventory management under asymmetric information. \citet{hasbrouck1991} pioneered the empirical vector autoregressive decomposition of trades and quotes, establishing that trade innovations exert persistent impacts on security prices. \citet{campbell1993trading} demonstrated that trading volume and return serial correlations reflect interactions between liquidity traders and risk-averse market makers.

numeric_source_review_queue.text: In modern electronic markets, high-frequency trading firms and automated algorithms dominate liquidity provision and execution \citep{menkveld2013,budish2015,biais2015}. While \citet{hendershott2011does} document that algorithmic trading improves liquidity and narrows bid-ask spreads during normal trading periods, \citet{budish2015} show that continuous double auctions generate socially wasteful latency arms races, and \citet{biais2015} demonstrate that algorithmic speed advantages can lead to adverse selection spirals. We advance this literature by formalizing the closed loop between algorithmic learning rules and endogenous price impact, establishing fundamental realization-theoretic bounds on what econometricians can infer from public ticker feeds.
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: A extensive literature examines the physics of price impact in electronic limit order books \citep{almgren2000,bouchaud2004fluctuations,cont2010stochastic,cont2014}. Empirical studies consistently reveal that signed order flow exhibits strong positive autocorrelation over hundreds of trades (long memory), while price returns remain approximately unpredictable \citep{bouchaud2004fluctuations,cont2014}. This apparent paradox is resolved by subtle negative feedback in quote replacement and cancellation. \citet{cont2014} introduce Order Flow Imbalance (OFI) as a powerful predictor of short-term price movements across multiple depth levels. We explicitly incorporate and control for order-splitting memory in our econometric models, demonstrating that even after purging 30 to 90 lags of signed flow memory, a positive and statistically significant feedback component persists in continuous high-frequency trading.
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: The distinction between market liquidity and funding liquidity is central to modern theories of financial fragility \citep{brunnermeier2009,adrian2010liquidity,he2013intermediary}. When leveraged market makers suffer balance-sheet drawdowns, risk-management constraints (such as Value-at-Risk limits or regulatory margin requirements) force them to withdraw quotes, widening spreads and amplifying price dislocations \citep{greenwood2015vulnerable,eisenberg2001systemic}. Our analysis demonstrates that non-normal transient amplification can trigger intermediary insolvency even when the underlying price-formation process is spectrally stable ($\rho(J) < 1$).
numeric_source_review_queue.classification: Numeric source text: may be a definition, methodological count, citation, literal result or claim; not automatically empirical

numeric_source_review_queue.text: In applied mathematics and fluid mechanics, non-normal linear systems have long been recognized as capable of explosive transient growth despite asymptotic eigenvalue decay \citep{kreiss1962,spijker1991,trefethen2005spectra}. While eigenvalues govern asymptotic behavior as $t \to \infty$, the pseudospectrum and the Kreiss constant determine short-term amplification. Although non-normal operator theory has been applied in macroeconomics to examine input-output networks, its application to high-frequency market microstructure and dealer solvency is novel. We derive the exact safe shock radius for leveraged dealers, prove tight bilateral bounds using Spijker's optimal constant, and demonstrate why spectral stability alone cannot guarantee intermediary solvency.

numeric_source_review_queue.text: We examine whether observable market data can identify destabilizing adaptive feedback between algorithms and financial prices, and whether dynamic eigenvalue stability guarantees financial safety. Our findings establish two fundamental results. First, observable feedback does not imply identifiable machine behavior: under the declared reset model with known anchor and impact, modeled price-state responses determine nonzero merged rate--weight representations rather than participant identities (Theorem~\ref{thm:m1_equivalence}), active probing to distinguish nearby adaptation rates faces a severe $\Omega(\delta^{-4})$ sample-complexity barrier (Theorem~\ref{thm:m2_sample_complexity}), and empirical feedback estimates are fragile artifacts of observation clocks and moving-average filtering. Second, dynamic price stability does not imply intermediary safety: because the closed-loop market Jacobian is generically non-normal, stable eigenvalues ($\rho(J) < 1$) can coexist with severe transient balance-sheet depletion governed by the exact loss radius $r^*_{\text{exact}} = B / \sup_{t \ge 0} \|C J^t\|_2$ and low-frequency variance accumulation under persistent flow. Because public surveillance faces intrinsic realization-theoretic limits near critical thresholds, our findings motivate capital-aware pre-trade gating.
